basics.name: Natalia L. Rubio
basics.summary: Currently employed at Stanford University. Ph.D. candidate in mechanical engineering at Stanford (NSF Graduate Research Fellow). Research at the intersection of machine learning, reduced-order modeling, and cardiovascular fluid mechanics.

work.company: physics-based acceleration of cardiovascular flow simulation — Stanford University (NSF Graduate Research Fellow
highlights: Supervisors: Prof. Alison Marsden, Prof. Eric Darve
Use ML to predict resistance and inductance for electric circuit surrogates that replace costly 3D finite-element cardiovascular simulations (minutes on a laptop vs. many hours on HPC).

Train models in JAX, PyTorch, and TensorFlow linking patient-specific vascular geometry to circuit parameters that reproduce high-fidelity 3D behavior; circuit analogs with learned parameters outperform heuristic resistances/inductances by roughly 50% error reduction.
Apply fluid-mechanics-informed modeling to reduce data needs (model form, non-dimensionalization, geometry discretization, feature selection).
Automate pipelines for geometry planning, meshing, and svMultiPhysics simulation for synthetic training data.
Optimize preprocessing, model architecture, and training choices; implement optimization for circuits with nonlinear ML components.
Maintain the [Vascular Model Repository](https://www.vascularmodel.com/); collaborate on GitHub; mentor junior students; organize [SimVascular](https://simvascular.github.io/) tutorials.

work.position: Implementation and comparison of graph neural network architectures — Pasteur Labs (Simulation Intelligence Intern)
highlights: Implemented graph-based ML surrogates for unsteady fluid dynamics; ran Azure experiments comparing latent-space approaches for memory and compute.

work.position: Variable-order fractional Laplacian for fractional Newtonian gravity — Stanford University (Ph.D. rotation)
highlights: Implemented a variable-order Riesz-potential method for fractional Poisson problems in MATLAB and Julia.

work.position: Corrosion of structural materials in liquid lead-bismuth eutectic (LBE) — UC Berkeley; Belgian Nuclear Research Centre (2017); Los Alamos National Laboratory (2018
highlights: Experiments and electron microscopy for LBE-cooled systems; finite-element advection–diffusion corrosion model in Python for closed-loop flows.
